cards.noteEn: Diagramas is plural. Although it ends in -a, diagrama is masculine: el diagrama and los diagramas.

example.en: The diagrams explain the process.

cards.answerEn: charts that turn a movie's character interactions into paths through time
cards.noteEn: Each line follows a character, and nearby lines show characters sharing a scene. The joke contrasts stories that form readable patterns with Primer, whose famously tangled time-travel plot becomes an almost indecipherable knot.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: On a diagram, líneas can refer to the drawn paths that trace people or things, rather than lines of written text.

example.es: Cada línea muestra una ruta distinta.
example.en: Each line shows a different route.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

example.en: What is your name?

cards.answerEn: they are (in a place or state)

cards.noteEn: Before a specific moment, en can correspond to English “at.”

example.en: He arrived at just the right moment.

cards.answerEn: belonging to; often expressed with ’s in English
cards.noteEn: De can connect a thing to its owner. Spanish says el libro de Ana where English can say ‘Ana’s book.’

example.en: It is Luis's computer.

cards.noteEn: Cima is the highest point of a mountain or, figuratively, the top position in a ranking.

example.es: Llegaron a la cima de la montaña.
example.en: They reached the summit of the mountain.

cards.noteEn: For the body-part sense, lengua means “tongue.” In a separate sense, lengua can mean “language.”

example.en: He bit his tongue.

cards.noteEn: De can join an invention, theorem, or named object to the person whose name it bears. English may instead use an adjective based on that name.

example.en: We study Newton's laws.

cards.noteEn: Used as a noun, muertos names people who are dead. Spanish can use an adjective with a plural article understood from context to refer to a group of people.

example.en: They remembered the dead.

cards.noteEn: Puerta can name a large defended gate as well as an ordinary door inside a building.

example.es: Cerraron la puerta de la fortaleza.
example.en: They closed the fortress gate.

cards.noteEn: Spanish writes de followed by the masculine singular word el as the single word del.

example.es: El color del coche es rojo.
example.en: The color of the car is red.

cards.noteEn: Rumbo names the direction in which someone or something is traveling. With a, it commonly introduces the destination.

example.en: The ship changed course.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is heading toward a destination?
cards.answerEn: Use rumbo a followed by the destination. Before el, a and el combine as al.
cards.noteEn: Rumbo means a course or heading, and a introduces the destination. The destination can be a place or a direction; only the form before el contracts, as in rumbo al norte.

example.es: El tren va rumbo a Sevilla.
example.en: The train is heading toward Seville.

cards.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.

example.en: I’m going to the market.

cards.noteEn: Oeste names the direction where the sun sets. This literal direction is distinct from el Oeste used as a broad cultural or geopolitical label.

example.es: El barco navega hacia el oeste.
example.en: The ship sails west.

cards.noteEn: Olifantes is the Spanish name for Tolkien's enormous elephant-like war animals.

example.en: The oliphaunts look like enormous elephants.

cards.noteEn: Ent is Tolkien's name for one of these beings; Spanish uses ents as the plural.

example.es: Los ents parecen árboles que caminan.
example.en: The Ents look like walking trees.

cards.noteEn: Hobbit is a fantasy name used in Spanish; its plural is hobbits.

example.es: Los hobbits viven en la Comarca.
example.en: The hobbits live in the Shire.

cards.noteEn: A trilogía is a set of three related works. Its written accent belongs on í.

example.en: I read the complete trilogy.

cards.noteEn: Estrella can mean an astronomical star or a famous performer. The surrounding words determine the sense.

example.en: That star is very far away.

cards.noteEn: Before el plus a masculine singular noun, todo means the whole amount or extent of it: todo el día, todo el trabajo.

example.en: She studied the whole chapter.

cards.answerEn: Jedi; relating to the Jedi Order
cards.noteEn: Spanish can use jedi as a noun or as an adjective after a noun; in adjective use, it describes something related to the Jedi Order.

example.es: El joven empezó su entrenamiento jedi.
example.en: The young man began his Jedi training.

cards.answerEn: on; against; introduces the target of an attack
cards.noteEn: After ataque, a can introduce the person or thing being attacked.

example.es: El ataque al castillo empezó de noche.
example.en: The attack on the castle began at night.

cards.noteEn: Coche commonly means “car” in Spain. Other Spanish-speaking regions may prefer carro or auto.

example.es: Hay muchos coches en la calle.
example.en: There are many cars in the street.

cards.noteEn: Raptor can be used as a shortened dinosaur name; this sense does not refer to a bird of prey.

example.es: El raptor corre hacia la puerta.
example.en: The raptor runs toward the door.

cards.noteEn: Niños can refer specifically to boys or more generally to a group of children whose members are male or mixed. The surrounding context decides which meaning is intended.

example.es: Los niños juegan en el patio.
example.en: The children are playing in the yard.

cards.answerEn: one must; it is necessary (as part of hay que)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something has to be done without naming who must do it?
cards.answerEn: Use hay que followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Hay que does not change for a person; it gives a general requirement, like English “one must,” “you have to,” or “we need to.”

example.en: Someone has to call tomorrow.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links hay to the required action

cards.noteEn: Lista can mean “ready” in other contexts. When it describes a person as an ability, it means “smart” or “clever.”

example.en: Marta is very smart.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; with comen, it emphasizes eating someone up
cards.noteEn: Comer means 'to eat.' With a matching short word such as me, te, or se, comerse can emphasize eating something completely.

example.es: Los niños se comen el pastel.
example.en: The children eat up the cake.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish emphasize reading, eating, or drinking a whole, clearly specified thing?
cards.answerEn: Choose me, te, se, nos, os, or se to match the person doing the action, and use it with the reading, eating, or drinking verb.
cards.noteEn: These small words can present the action as carried through over the complete book, meal, drink, or stated amount; they do not mean that the person acts on themselves. Compare leer un libro, “read a book,” with leerse un libro, which often suggests reading it through. The small word normally goes before a verb form that shows person and time, as in se leyó; it attaches to an unchanged dictionary form, as in leerse. This completion nuance is not required every time.

example.es: Ana se leyó la novela en dos días.
example.en: Ana read through the novel in two days.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

example.en: I see Marta.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

example.en: I know Marta.
